verses.1: Their reckoning is near, yet mankind turns away in heedlessness.
verses.2: They hear every new reminder from their Lord while at play.
verses.3: Al-Mizan states: With distracted hearts, the unjust secretly say: He is only a mortal like you; will you knowingly submit to enchantment?
verses.4: Al-Mizan states: He said: My Lord knows all speech in heaven and earth; He is the Hearing, the Knowing.
verses.5: Al-Mizan states: They call it dream-medleys, forgery, or poetry, and demand a sign like those sent with earlier prophets.
verses.6: No town We destroyed had believed before them; will they then believe?
verses.7: Al-Mizan states: Before you We sent only men who received revelation; ask the people of the reminder if you do not know.
verses.8: We did not make them bodies that needed no food, nor did they abide forever.
verses.9: Al-Mizan states: We fulfilled Our promise, delivered them and whom We wished, and destroyed the extravagant.
verses.10: Al-Mizan states: We revealed to you a Book containing their reminder; will they not understand?
verses.11: Al-Mizan states: We shattered many iniquitous towns and raised another people after them.
verses.12: When they sensed Our might, they fled.
verses.13: Al-Mizan states: Do not flee; return to your luxury and dwellings, perhaps you will be questioned.
verses.14: They confessed: Woe to us; we were unjust.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan states that the chapter establishes prophethood on the basis of monotheism and resurrection. It opens by warning that reckoning is near while people neglect revelation, the standard by which they will be judged. The deniers mock the Prophet as a human enchanter and call his message dream-medleys, fabrication, or poetry; the chapter answers by showing that the former prophets shared his human characteristics and brought the same kind of divine message. It then recounts the histories of many prophets, from Moses and Aaron to Zachariah, John, and Jesus, before returning to the Reckoning, the respective ends of sinners and the God-fearing, the inheritance of the earth by God’s righteous servants, and proofs of monotheism. Its threats and warnings outweigh its promises, and its Meccan character is unanimously recognized by its content and context.

The commentary explains that iqtaraba intensifies the sense of nearness more than qaruba. In “to mankind,” the lām has the sense of ilā: the reckoning is moving toward and seeking people, rather than being measured from them. Reckoning means God’s actual accounting of deeds on the Day of Resurrection, not merely its time. Although some take proximity and distance to apply only to time and therefore supply “the time of reckoning,” the context calls people to attend to the accounting for which they are responsible; if the point were the terrors of the Hour, the verse would have mentioned the day of reckoning instead.

“People” means the whole human society, though those not marked by heedlessness, turning away, and mockery are excepted. This is not a metaphorical generalization from a majority to all, but a literal social attribution qualified by exceptions. Some explain the nearness of reckoning by the world’s daily advance toward its last day, or by the Prophet’s mission at the end of time. The former suits a continuing expression, whereas iqtaraba is past tense; the past may instead express the certainty of what will occur.

Their heedlessness arises from absorption in worldly affairs and pleasures, which fills their hearts and leaves no room for an awakening remembrance of reckoning. Ghaflah includes both failing to notice something and noticing it without its affecting the soul. Thus it does not conflict with their “turning aside”: they know of the reckoning but worldly preoccupation prevents them from taking that knowledge seriously or preparing through repentance, faith, and avoidance of evil. Al-Zamakhsharī treats heedlessness and turning aside as successive stages—first neglect, then refusal when warnings come—but Al-Mizan holds that the verse apparently describes two simultaneous qualities. Other attempts to make “turning aside” mean extensive heedlessness, or to reduce heedlessness to negligence, unnecessarily restrict the wording.

Verses (21:2-3) explain this heedlessness. The unconnected new sentence gives its explanation: had they not been heedless and turning away, they would not treat a reminder meant to prepare them as play. The reminder is revelation and scripture, including the Qur’an; its coming means its revelation to the Prophet, his communication of it, and their hearing it. Muḥdath, “new,” is relative: the Qur’an is new after the Gospel, the Gospel after the Torah, and later Qur’anic passages are new in relation to earlier ones. The wording confines their state on hearing every new reminder to playing and having distracted hearts. Laʿib is a purposive-looking activity with no end beyond imagination, like children’s games, whereas lahw is the heart’s diversion from what should concern it. Hence renewed reminders have no effect whatever: they neither withdraw them from worldly play nor make them mindful of what awaits them; the implication is not that old reminders affect them.

The literal wording has been cited for the createdness of the Qur’an. The Ashʿairite response—that its revelation is created while it is inherently eternal—is contrary to the verse’s apparent meaning. Al-Mizan argues more broadly that ordinary speech, composed of successively produced sounds and conventionally assigned signs, has no independent external reality as “speech.” Repetitions and reports of the same words are new sounds, called the same speech only by convention because they convey the same intended meaning. Speech in this direct sense therefore cannot properly be described as originated, enduring, or eternal, qualities belonging to external realities. Moreover, eternality is impossible for a sequence of letters whose parts precede and follow one another: it would make subsequent parts both originated and eternal.

Strictly speaking, speech is neither a real action proceeding from an essence nor an essential attribute of a speaker, because it is a conventional construct. Yet, since its uttered sounds are real actions, speech is treated by extension as an action, and “speaker” as an attribute derived from that relation. If speech is analyzed through its function of revealing what is hidden, it may be used in a real and wider sense: every effect discloses its cause, and a thing’s essential attributes disclose its essence. In this sense God’s knowledge, power, and life, and indeed the world, may be called His speech. God’s knowledge is eternal speech because it is identical with His eternal Essence; created things are originated speech as signs of God; and revelation is originated as God’s act of teaching, while eternal insofar as it belongs to His eternal knowledge.

Thus the recited Qur’anic verses, as sounds indicating meanings, cannot literally be called either originated or eternal, though their sounds are originated. Their meanings are eternal only in the sense that God’s knowledge of them is eternal, just as His knowledge of every thing is eternal. The dispute over the Qur’an’s origination or eternality is consequently futile, and speech is not an additional affirmative essential attribute beside knowledge; otherwise countless analyzable perfections would become separate attributes. In religious and Qur’anic usage, kalām normally retains its direct sense of sequentially uttered words. The proposal of an eternal “inherent speech” distinct from uttered speech fails: if it means the meanings or their mental forms, it is simply knowledge, while if it means something else, it is inconceivable from human experience. A poetical assertion about speech residing in the heart has no force in this intellectual inquiry.

The unjust alone conceal their counsels; such conspiracies cannot literally be attributed to all the people, among whom were the disadvantaged and those unconcerned with them. Their secrecy concerns their prior deliberation over how to oppose the Prophet’s call, though they later voiced their rejection publicly. They argue that, since he is visibly a mortal like themselves and has no manifest distinction from them, his alleged connection with the unseen must be impossible: if it were possible for him, it should be possible for them. From this they conclude that what he brings is not a divine sign but enchantment, to which no clear-sighted person should submit.

The Prophet’s reply refers the matter wholly to God: He knows every word in heaven and earth, whether secret or public; He hears what they say and knows what they do. This is the same way prophets answer demands for a desired miracle: its knowledge and disposal belong to God, not to the messenger.

Their claims in verse (21:5) escalate. “Medleys of dreams” charges the Prophet with mistaking a confused dream for revelation; “he has forged it” charges deliberate invention; and “he is a poet” is still more disparaging, for poetic speech is portrayed as the unreflective product of imagination and emotion, capable of praising evil, denouncing good, affirming falsehood, or denying truth. Having rejected the Qur’an as a proof of prophecy, they demand a sign like those with which the former prophets were sent. The phrase “were sent” implies that a sign is a necessary accompaniment of a true mission. Yet their demand exposes their confusion and contradiction: people who categorically deny prophethood appeal to earlier prophets and their signs. It also contains an implied promise that they would believe if such a sign came.

Verse (21:6) rejects that promise as false. Earlier towns demanded signs, received them, and still disbelieved; their final outcome was destruction. If these people, alike in extravagance and arrogance, were given their requested signs, they likewise would not believe and would be destroyed. The verse therefore implicitly says that none of the former inhabitants of towns who demanded and received such signs believed, and that destruction followed their persistent unbelief.

The statement that earlier messengers were only men receiving revelation answers the objection based on the Prophet’s mortality. It first refutes the objection by precedent: being human does not conflict with prophethood, since former prophets were human. It then resolves it constructively: revelation is a special divine gift, not a universal quality such that its absence in one person proves its absence in all. “Ask the people of the reminder” reinforces the historical point. The reminder here is scripture, and its people are the People of the Book, whom the polytheists respected, consulted, and used to test the Prophet despite their shared hostility to him. The challenge addresses the Prophet and all listeners, learned and ignorant alike, to confirm that former prophets were human.

Those messengers had ordinary human needs: they ate food and did not remain forever. God then fulfilled His promise to support their religion and establish their call to the truth, delivering the messengers and believers whom He willed while destroying the extravagant polytheists who exceeded the bounds of servitude. The Qur’an is, in turn, God’s favor to this entire community: it is their fitting reminder, containing the highest truths and teachings human capacity can receive and the most sound laws for society. The interpretation of their “remembrance” as merely their honor if they hold fast to the Book is unlikely.

Finally, “town” means its inhabitants. God shattered towns whose people wronged themselves through unbelief and extravagance, then brought another people after them. When those inhabitants sensed the divine punishment, they fled like a routed army. They are mockingly told to return to their luxurious ease and homes, so that the poor might again come begging and they might resume their arrogance, pomp, and concealment from them. The command portrays their conceit and their assumption of lordship over the masses instead of recognizing God’s lordship. Their cry, “O woe to us! Surely we were unjust,” is a regretful admission of God’s Lordship and their wrongdoing. It continues until they are made like a harvested crop: extinguished and silent like a dying fire, with neither sound nor surviving name or fame.
verses.16: God did not create the heavens, the earth, and what lies between them for sport.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says that, had God wished diversion, He would have made it from before Himself—if He were to do so.
verses.18: Al-Mizan states that God hurls truth against falsehood, breaks its head, and it vanishes; woe is due for what they describe.
verses.19: Al-Mizan states that all in the heavens and earth are His, while those with Him neither disdain serving Him nor grow weary.
verses.20: They glorify Him night and day without languor.
verses.21: Have they taken earthly gods who raise the dead?
verses.22: Al-Mizan says that gods besides Allah would disorder heaven and earth; Allah, Lord of the Throne, is above their attributions.
verses.23: God is not questioned concerning what He does, but they shall be questioned.
verses.24: Al-Mizan challenges them to prove gods besides Him; the reminders with the Prophet and before him oppose the claim, but most turn aside from the truth they do not know.
verses.25: Al-Mizan says that every earlier messenger received the revelation: there is no god but Me; therefore, serve Me.
verses.26: Al-Mizan says: They claim the Beneficent has a son; glory be to Him—rather, they are honored servants.
verses.27: Al-Mizan says that they do not speak before Him and act only by His command.
verses.28: Al-Mizan says that He knows what is before and behind them; they intercede only for one He approves, and they tremble in fear of Him.
verses.29: Al-Mizan states that whoever among them claims divinity besides Him will be repaid with Hell, the recompense of the unjust.
verses.30: Al-Mizan asks disbelievers to see that the heavens and earth were closed, then opened, and that every living thing was made of water; will they not believe?
verses.31: Al-Mizan states that great mountains were made in the earth lest it convulse with them, and wide ways in it so that they may follow a right direction.
verses.32: Al-Mizan states that heaven was made a guarded canopy, yet they turn aside from its signs.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains these verses as justifying the punishment of former iniquitous towns and proving Resurrection, from which the necessity of prophethood follows. Human beings are not left free to play as they please: they return to their Lord, are reckoned and requited for their deeds, and wrongdoers are punished. Creation cannot be purposeless, for that would make it sport and diversion.

Laʿib is an orderly act with an imaginary rather than real end, such as children's games; insofar as it distracts from real work, it is also lahw, diversion. A purposeless world would mean bringing things into being and annihilating them, giving life and death, building and destroying merely to keep busy or relieve boredom, need, loneliness, or some other deficiency. Such diversion through creation is impossible for God, because creation is His act and external to His Essence; what wholly depends on Him cannot affect Him or fulfill a need in Him. Thus, if diversion were supposed, it would have to be “from before Ourselves,” namely within the level of the Essence rather than through created action. Yet diversion within the Essence would itself entail need and deficiency. The verses principally establish that there is no sport in God's creative action; the impossible conditional law, reinforced by “if We were to do (so),” indirectly also negates diversion in the Essence. “From before Ourselves” therefore justifies the denial that creation is sport.

Creation's purpose is Resurrection: people are returned, judged, and rewarded or punished. Resurrection in turn requires prophethood and a true call that distinguishes sound belief and righteous action from their opposites. Without Resurrection, creation would be futile; since creation is not futile, Resurrection follows, and with it prophethood. The commentary rejects readings of “from before Ourselves” as “by Our power,” since power does not attach to impossibilities and the phrase does not mean power; as an unseen diversion concealed because it is shameful, since fear of disclosure presupposes weakness and makes the interpretation self-contradictory; and as wife or children, since this breaks the connection with the argument. The suggestion that a divine “diversion” would necessarily be wisdom is correct in itself but not the wording's apparent sense. The final in is conditional, not negative; its omitted consequence is understood from the preceding clause.

The commentary explains that truth has fixed reality, whereas falsehood has no fixed reality and only resembles truth, like a mirage resembling water. True beliefs accord with reality; the Hereafter is truth, while the worldly possessions and powers on which people rely are falsehood; God is truth, whereas other supposed independent means and forces are falsehood. Truth is attributable to God, but falsehood, as falsehood, is not: it arises from limitation and deficiency when things are compared with what is more perfect, and is attributable to Him only by permission. Apart from God, everything has some admixture of falsehood.

God's continuing custom is to give falsehood respite until truth confronts it, then to cast truth upon it so that falsehood suddenly and utterly perishes. The present tense of “We hurl” denotes this ongoing custom; the image of striking its head shows truth's superiority. The verse is unrestricted: a true argument destroys false belief, and exterminatory punishment may eradicate false practices. It is not about earnestness prevailing over an actually existing divine diversion, since diversion has been denied of God altogether. Its warning concerns those who deny Resurrection. Ultimately God establishes and purifies truth until only sheer truth remains, and all supposed independent power, possession, and authority of other-than-God vanish.

All who are in the heavens and earth belong to God through real ownership inseparable from their creation: every created thing depends on its Existentiator and cannot escape His command. This answers any claim that some people might not be His property and thus escape return, reckoning, and requital. “Those who are with Him” are beings granted special proximity and awareness of His presence, perhaps the favored angels, though the expression is not limited to them. They neither arrogantly refuse service nor cease from weariness, but glorify Him incessantly.

Unlike human lordship, which rests on mutual need and may lighten obligations for favored servants, God's real lordship entails no need on His part and complete need on the part of what He owns. The nearer and more favored a servant is, the more God's greatness and his own need become manifest to him, and the more deeply he serves. Hence proximity grants no exemption from service, reckoning, or requital; even the honored servants glorify without ceasing.

The question about gods “from the earth” refutes the thought that other gods could raise the dead and reckon people, making worship of God unnecessary. It may point out that earthly gods are themselves subject to death and resurrection, or disparage idols made from earthly materials. The angels whom idolaters take as gods are themselves God's servants; turning from them to earthly representations cannot provide help in the Hereafter.

The dispute with the idolaters is not about whether the Necessary Being and Creator is one, for they accepted that. It concerns lordship and worship: they supposed that God had delegated the regulation of distinct regions and classes of the universe to transcendent beings, which should therefore be worshiped as intercessors. The verse denies multiple gods as regulators and objects of worship, not multiple creators; being a god “in” heaven or earth means having authority over it, not residing there.

If there were genuinely multiple gods, they would differ in essence and consequently in their regulation; the order of heaven and earth would then be spoiled. But the universe's systems are harmonious, ordered, and directed to a common end, so their regulating source is one. Competing causes within the one cosmic system do not invalidate this proof: they may limit one another while jointly yielding the system's result, like the opposed scales of a balance serving its owner's measurement. Nor can multiple regulators be imagined to agree rationally on a common order, because rational rules are abstracted from the external order; in the case of the universe's lord, that external order is His act and cannot govern Him. This is a demonstrative proof, not merely a popular persuasive argument. The Throne denotes dominion, and the verse clears God of the attribution of other gods who resurrect or regulate His kingdom.

The nearest contextual sense of “He is not questioned concerning what He does, but they shall be questioned” is that the supposed gods are accountable whereas God is not. Exegetes explain the first clause by God's absolute wisdom, since His acts have decisive benefit while others' acts may be beneficial or harmful. Others infer that His acts have no motivating gharaḍ, because He needs no perfection external to Himself; still others ascribe the absence of questioning to His overwhelming might. The commentary holds that mere fear of a tyrant's might is not the intended meaning, and that wisdom is true but too general and insufficiently grounded in the clause itself.

The more plausible explanation follows the preceding designation, “Lord of the Throne”: God has absolute dominion and ownership over all things, so He may dispose of His property as He wills, whereas they have no such independent right and are answerable. His acts are nevertheless wise, good, and beneficial, so no evil should be suspected of them. Dominion also gives the verse its link with the surrounding argument: unanswerability proves His all-encompassing dominion, dominion proves His lordship and ownership, and creatures' accountability proves that they are not lords.

For voluntary human action, a mental apprehension of an act's good and benefit motivates action, and an agent is wise when his action corresponds to the external order represented in this mental map. A question asking why someone acted asks for this correspondence and the benefit motivating him. God's acts, however, are the external reality to which other acts and mental maps must conform; they are wisdom itself. Benefit follows His acts, but no pre-existing benefit motivates Him. Thus His acts cannot be measured against another external system or questioned as to how they conform to truth: His act is itself the truth.

The commentary rejects the view that things possess subsistence before existence, with intrinsic goods, evils, benefits, and potentialities known by God prior to creation. It wrongly makes God's detailed knowledge acquired and consequent upon the known, whereas His knowledge is presential; it treats non-existent things as subsisting although thingness and existence are inseparable; and it attributes potentiality, actuality, perfection, deficiency, and benefit to something supposedly prior to external existence. God's word and act are instead the external existence of things, and true speech or belief is true by conforming to that reality, which originates from Him.

The demand, “Bring your proof,” challenges the unsupported adoption of gods besides Him. Dhikr means either the revealed Book—the Qur'an for those with the Prophet and the scriptures of earlier prophets—or, more specifically, what revelation teaches concerning divinity and worship. Both the Qur'an and prior revelation affirm that God alone is divine and alone must be worshiped. Most opponents do not distinguish truth from falsehood or follow proof, and therefore turn away. The statement that every messenger received the revelation that there is no god but God confirms this second sense of dhikr; the continuous verbal form indicates the ongoing character of this revelation, and “serve Me” addresses both messengers and their communities.

The claim that the Beneficent has taken a son concerns the idolaters' claim about angels. God is declared far above it, and the angels are identified as honored servants. Their honor is precisely perfect servitude: they see themselves only as servants, and God has honored them by granting them this state. Human honor is acquired, whereas angelic honor is not, although divine honoring is grace in both cases.

They do not precede God in speech: their speech follows His, and this may allude to their wills following His will. The prior placement of “according to His command” makes their action exclusive to that command; they act and speak in absolute obedience. They neither will nor do anything other than what He wills, which is complete servitude. Since command is opposed to prohibition, the wording implies that angels know no prohibition, for prohibition concerns the possibility of committing what is forbidden, while they act only upon command.

The usual explanation of “He knows what is before them and what is behind them” as their past and future deeds does not adequately explain their acting only by His command and assumes an awareness not stated in the verse. The preferable interpretation is that what is before them comprises the acts and effects subsequent to their existence, and what is behind them comprises the antecedent causes and origins of that existence. God thus knows both their noble source and their praiseworthy words and deeds, explaining their honor and obedience.

Their intercession, which idolaters invoked to justify worshiping angels, is only for one whose religion God approves. Since associating partners with God is not forgiven, the approved person is a monotheist, not an idolater. The angels fear God's wrath and punishment although their divinely bestowed infallibility secures them from disobedience and punishment. Their security does not diminish His dominion or power. The warning that any of them who claimed divinity would receive Hell is a conditional proposition and does not imply that its condition has occurred.

The final signs demonstrate God's exclusive lordship by showing that creation and the regulation of affairs are inseparable. The idolaters assigned creation to God but regulation to other gods; the formation and ordered condition of heaven, earth, life, mountains, pathways, heaven, night, day, sun, and moon expose the error. “Seeing” here is intellectual observation made evident by reflection on tangible phenomena. Ratq is joining and fatq is separating: heaven and earth were joined and then separated. The continual separation of compounds, plants, animals, and human beings into distinct forms whose properties had existed only potentially in their undifferentiated matter indicates an original unity and a divinely ordered differentiation. The same governing rule applies to earthly and heavenly material things, even though human lifespans do not permit observation of celestial cycles. Thus existence and regulation are joined in one comprehensive system; contemporary scientific discoveries about common physical elements support this observation.

A second possible reading is that heaven was closed so it gave no rain and earth was closed so it produced no vegetation, then both were opened by rain and growth. This is also a complete proof and is supported by the following reference to water, though narrower than the first explanation. The reading that they were indistinct in pre-existence and then became distinct after non-existence correctly proves an Originator in itself, but does not answer idolaters who already admitted God as Creator; what must be shown to them is that regulation likewise belongs to Him. Making every living thing from water means that water has an important role in the creation of living beings, and the sign's setting among visible phenomena may exclude angels and similar beings.

Rawāsiya are firmly fixed mountains, made so the earth would not convulse with its inhabitants; the verse suggests a close connection between mountains and earthquakes. Fijājan subulan are broad roads between mountains, enabling people to reach their destinations and homes. The guarded heaven apparently means that it is protected from devils, while its signs are heavenly events displaying one regulation and one source.

Finally, each of night, day, sun, and moon has its own falak, or celestial sphere, in which it swiftly travels. Night is the conical shadow attached to the earth on the side opposite the sun, and day its opposite. The verse concerns terrestrial and atmospheric conditions: the sun and other fixed luminaries have no day or night, while the moon and other bodies that receive light have conditions different from earthly day and night. Yasbaḥūna derives from sabḥ, passing through water by splitting it, or swimming; the rational plural form has been explained by the use of swimming as an act of rational beings.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as a continuation of the discussion of prophethood. They answer the polytheists’ hope that the Prophet’s death would free them from his call and criticism of their gods, their derision of him, and their mockery of the threatened Resurrection. They warn and threaten the deniers while consoling the Prophet.

No mortal, including the Prophet, was granted eternal life; but his death will not benefit the deniers or make them eternal, for every person dies, undergoes divine trial during an appointed life, returns to God, and is recompensed. The rhetorical question, “if you die, will they live forever?”, rejects their implied fantasy that the Prophet alone prevents their lasting, carefree existence. Since worldly life is a finite period of testing, it cannot be endless: trial is preparatory and must be followed by return to God and decisive requital.

The verses portray the deniers as treating the Prophet only with mockery, indignantly defending idols while denying remembrance of the Beneficent; as hasty in demanding the signs of punishment; and as challenging the Prophet and believers about the threatened event. They will be unable to repel the Fire from before or behind them, receive no help, and be overtaken suddenly, confounded, unable to avert or postpone it. The fate of communities that mocked earlier messengers warns them that the punishment they deride will befall them.

They have no protector from the Beneficent by night or day and no gods capable even of helping or defending themselves. Their prolonged enjoyment of provision, shared with their fathers, has deluded them, though God removes nations from the earth and can likewise destroy them. The Prophet warns only by certain revelation, but their own deafness prevents them from heeding it; even a slight touch of punishment would make them confess their injustice. On the Day of Resurrection, just balances will ensure that no deed, even one of mustard-seed weight, escapes God’s accounting.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan holds that nafs has three relevant usages. Originally, when annexed to another word, it means the very thing to which it is annexed and, when used for emphasis, functions like a reflexive pronoun; in this sense it may be applied to anything, even God. It later came to mean an individual human being composed of spirit and body, and subsequently the human spirit specifically, as the basis of life, knowledge, and strength.

The latter two meanings are not ordinary lexical usages for plants or other animals, apart from specialized terminology; blood may exceptionally be called nafs because life depends on it. Nor are they lexically used for angels or jinn, although jinn have duties, die, and are resurrected. Mawt means the loss of life and such properties as feeling and volition by something capable of them. Philosophical definitions of death as the soul’s departure from the body, or a transmitted description of it as passage from one abode to another, are not its ordinary lexical meaning.

Human beings are subject to death through their bodies, which possess life and then lose it; the verse does not attribute death to the spirit, nor does it establish that mawt applies to angels. Halāk and ṣaʿq, though sometimes concomitant with death, differ from mawt. Therefore, in “Every nafs shall taste of death,” nafs means the human person (insān), not the spirit, and the verse concerns humankind alone, not angels, jinn, animals, or plants. Its preceding reference to mortal man and its following reference to testing by evil and good confirm this restriction.

The commentary rejects interpretations that make nafs here rūḥ or extend the verse to every living being. It also criticizes Imam al-Rāzī’s universal reading in al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr: the annexed, reflexive sense of nafs that may be applied to God is unavailable here because nafs is unannexed; the claim that inanimate things do not die conflicts with Qur’anic usage; and the verse cannot refute philosophical claims about immortal spirits, immaterial intellects, and celestial souls. Such claims stand or fall by demonstrative proof (burhān): if demonstratively established, a text’s speculative apparent meaning cannot oppose them; if not, they need no speculative textual refutation.

“Every person shall taste of death” confirms that no mortal has everlasting life and introduces the testing of human beings by disliked conditions such as illness and poverty, and favored conditions such as health and wealth. Each person has a limited lifespan of such trial and then returns to God for judgment for or against him. Death is inevitable precisely because life is a preparatory trial: what is preparatory cannot continue without end, but must be followed by the stage in which its result is decided.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains that in is negative: when the disbelievers see the Prophet, their entire manner of dealing with him is mockery and derision. Their unspoken phrase is, in effect, “they say: Is this he who speaks of your gods?” Their derogatory wording means that he speaks ill of their gods, though they omit “ill” out of courtesy toward them.

The clause about their denial of the remembrance of the Beneficent most likely qualifies this implied “they say.” They are offended on behalf of idols because the Prophet truthfully denies that the idols can benefit or harm, and they answer him with scorn; yet they themselves deny the remembrance of God and feel no indignation at it. This remembrance means remembering God as the source of all mercy and blessings, which necessarily entails worshipping Him as Lord; it has also been interpreted as the Qur’an.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan says that, beyond rejecting the prophetic call, the polytheists’ continual mockery of the Prophet was further disbelief and insolence. Mockery treats its object as frivolous, but God does not regard mockery of His Prophet and Book as a trivial matter. Their disbelief followed by mockery therefore exposes them to punishment twice and effectively constitutes a demand that its signs be hastened. Unpersuaded by signs given in ease, they demand signs that will requite their deeds; God promises soon to show them such punitive signs.

“Man is created of haste” expresses humanity’s extreme haste as though haste were its very substance. It is an exclamatory, disdainful expression, not merely a statement that people are very hasty, and implies that God’s delay of punishment does not put them beyond His reach. Here, “I will show you My signs” means punishment with Hellfire, as the following verse indicates.
verses.38: Al-Mizan explains that the disbelievers address both the Prophet and the believers. Instead of the expected singular kunta, “if you are truthful,” they use the plural kuntum in order both to challenge the Prophet with a demand he cannot fulfill at their bidding and to mislead the believers and turn them against him. The threatened event they demand is alluded to in the preceding verse and explained in the next.
verses.39: Al-Mizan explains that law expresses a wish: it is wished that the disbelievers knew the time when they could not ward off the Fire. It will seize them from before and behind, indicating that they are surrounded by it. Nor can they repel it either by themselves or through anyone else’s help. Thus the verse answers their question about the appointed threat by wishing that they knew the time of their helplessness before the Fire.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan holds that “it shall come upon them” refers contextually to Hellfire, not, as some exegetes suggest, to the Hour. The verse follows their inability to ward off the Fire; proposed explanations based on an omitted statement or on the preceding wish do not fit the context.

Its sudden coming means that the Fire will surprise them: they will not know whence it comes or how it surrounds them. Unlike worldly fire, which moves gradually from exterior to interior and from place to place, the Fire of Hell takes hold of a person inwardly and outwardly alike. It gives no opportunity to flee, turn away, erect a barrier, or find refuge, for it is not confined to a direction and is as inseparable from them as their souls. Hence, and God knows best, it strikes from where they least expect; they are astonished and confused, unable to repel or delay it.
verses.41: Al-Mizan reports that Majmaʿ al-bayān distinguishes huzʾ, degrading someone through speech, from sukhriyyah, humiliating someone; taskhīr means humiliation or subjugation. Hayq means “to befall,” and what the disbelievers mocked was punishment. The verse consoles the Prophet and warns and threatens the disbelievers: earlier messengers too were mocked, until the punishment they ridiculed befell their scoffers.
verses.42: Al-Mizan explains kilāʾah as protection. The question asks who could protect the deniers from the Beneficent if He willed to punish them. Their turning away from the remembrance of their Lord shows that warning and admonition do not affect them: they neither attend to nor listen to the Qur’an when it is recited. Dhikr has also been interpreted as any admonition and proof.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains that am is disconnected from the preceding statement, not an alternative parallel to it, and that the rhetorical question negates that the polytheists possess gods besides God who can defend them from Him. On this reading, tamnaʿuhum and min dūninā describe the alleged gods: min dūninā means “besides Us,” while protection from God is implied. An alternative reading takes min dūninā as “from Us” and leaves “other than God” implied.

The following statement justifies the negation without a conjunction. Their gods cannot assist themselves—that is, cannot help one another—and are not themselves protected from God; therefore they cannot protect their worshippers. The view that the plural pronouns refer to the polytheists rather than to the gods does not suit the context.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s continual provision for the polytheists and their fathers prolonged the life of their society, deluded them, made them forget God’s remembrance, and turned them from His service. This was the condition of Quraysh: after Ishmael they lived safely in the ḥaram with abundant provisions, but, after taking Mecca and expelling Jurhum, abandoned Abraham’s religion and worshipped idols.

The interpretation most fitting the context takes God’s shrinking of the land’s sides to mean the extinction of its nations. Just as every nation has an appointed term, nation after nation is removed by God’s command. The verse asks what could prevent the polytheists from likewise perishing, and whether they could prevail if God willed them harm, destruction, or extinction.
verses.45: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet’s warning is divine revelation, in which there is no doubt. Its failure to guide the hearers arises from their own deafness to warning, not from any deficiency in the revelation.
verses.46: Al-Mizan explains nafḥah as an incident of punishment. Warnings conveyed through the verses of the reminder, the Qur’an, do not avail these people; only a blast of punishment compels them to believe and confess that they were unjust.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains al-qisṭ as justice or fairness. Its relation to al-mawāzīn may be interpretive—“balances of justice”—or adjectival through an implied expression, “balances possessed of justice.”

The clause about a mustard seed concerns the deed being weighed: even if its weight equals that minute amount, God will bring it forth for reckoning. Mustard-seed weight conventionally signifies extreme smallness and insignificance, affirming that no deed escapes God’s sufficient account on the Day of Resurrection.

verses.74: Al-Mizan states that God gave Lot wisdom and knowledge and delivered him from a town of evil, transgressing people who committed abominations.

verses.77:
Al-Mizan presents these passages as continuing the proof of religious legislation after the discussion of prophethood founded on resurrection. Through accounts of prophets given wisdom and religious law and delivered from their oppressors, they warn polytheists and give believers good news. The chapter names seventeen prophets in all; the present verses concern Moses, Aaron, Abraham, Lot, Isaac, Jacob, and Noah, with Noah preceding the others.

The Criterion, light, and reminder given to Moses and Aaron are the Torah. It distinguishes truth from falsehood in belief and action, illuminates the path to happiness in this world and the Hereafter, and recalls God through its admonitions and lessons. The definite al-furqān may be a proper name of the Torah; alternatively, the Torah is a criterion for everyone, while only the God-conscious benefit from it as light and reminder. The blessed reminder revealed in verse (21:50) is the Qur’an. Its blessing is its abundant, enduring good, which benefits human society even when people deny it, do not recognize its form, or—among Muslims—neglect it. Abraham’s prior rectitude means the special, innate disposition by which, according to his capacity known fully to God, he reached monotheism and other truths without instruction, reminder, or prompting.

Abraham’s question about the images concerns the idols to which his father and people devoted themselves in worship. Their answer makes inherited custom their justification; hence he calls both them and their fathers manifestly astray, because what they serve can neither benefit nor harm. Their question whether he is serious or joking displays the surprise of blind followers when their inherited belief is challenged. He answers that their Lord is the Creator and Lord of heaven and earth: this refutes their notion that God is only the God of gods and Lord of lords, rather than their own God and the God of the heavens and earth, and establishes monotheism. His testimony signifies not mere knowledge but practical adherence, completing his assurance that he is in earnest. The commentary rejects other interpretations that do not fit either the course of the verses or the idolaters’ beliefs.

His oath to plot against the idols is apparently an expression of firm intention rather than a public declaration. Kayd is a secret harmful scheme, and their departure perhaps indicates a festival or similar occasion that left the place empty. Since this was the beginning of Abraham’s call among powerful, fanatical idolaters, it would have been imprudent to announce such a plan openly, though he may have told persons unlikely to spread it. He shattered the idols but left their chief intact. The phrase that they might return to it apparently portrays the action as that of one who leaves a survivor to be blamed for the others’ destruction; thus the pronoun refers to the chief idol. Readings that make it refer to Abraham or to God render the exception of the chief idol superfluous.

The people seek the perpetrator in remorse and condemn him as unjust, believing that he violated the gods’ claimed right to reverence, the people’s right to have their sacred things honored, and his own proper limits. Hearing that Abraham had spoken ill of the idols, they summon him before a public gathering, apparently so witnesses can establish this and induce his confession, not merely to watch his punishment. Their question determines who acted, while calling the idols “our gods” shows that they did not count Abraham among their worshipers.

Abraham’s statement that the chief did it is not literal but a debating argument intended to force a concession. The unbroken chief amid the smashed idols sets up his command that they ask the idols, if they can speak. It thereby leads them to concede that their gods cannot speak, without positing omitted words or a displaced order in the verse. Alternative explanations—making the condition qualify the chief’s action or supplying an omitted subject—are contrived. The people then examine themselves and recognize individually that they are unjust for worshiping insensate objects. But they reverse the truth that has become clear, again accuse Abraham of injustice, and say that he knows the idols cannot speak.

Abraham does not defend himself, since his purpose is to refute the idols’ divinity. Their inability to speak entails that they neither know nor act; therefore they can neither benefit nor harm. Worship, being grounded in hope of good or fear of evil, is futile toward such beings. His condemnation expresses dissociation from them and their gods, and his question reproaches their failure to understand. Although his argument means that breaking idols is not an injustice, he does not expressly deny the charge; they therefore judge him guilty, call for him to be burned, and urge one another to help their gods by punishing their insulter.

God’s command to the fire was a takwīnī command: through an extraordinary miracle, its burning and destructive properties became coolness and peace for Abraham. Since rational analysis of natural events relies on recurring, known causal links, the underlying connections of miracles cannot be fully analyzed in this way, though the soul’s attention and determination have some relation to them. The unconnected wording, “We said,” answers the implied question of what followed after Abraham was cast into the fire. Their scheme aimed to extinguish his light and invalidate his proof, but it failed and was followed by his domination over them through divine protection and deliverance.

The blessed land to which Abraham and Lot were delivered is the Levant; Lot was the first to believe in Abraham and fled with him. Nāfilah means a gift, referring to Isaac and Jacob. The imamate of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob apparently concerns its placement in Abraham’s progeny. Guiding by God’s command is not merely showing the way, for Abraham received imamate after prophethood, which already entails such guidance. It is taking people to their destination through generative, inward influence that advances souls through spiritual stations. The command is therefore not legislative but the creative command by which a thing is brought into being.

The Imam must first possess this guidance, which then reaches people according to their capacities. He is the link through which inward divine effusions reach them, just as the prophet conveys outward effusions, namely divine law. Prophethood and imamate may thus be joined, as in Abraham and his two sons. The wording “the doing of good,” prayer, and alms uses a maṣdar that signifies the realized occurrence of acts, not a future command. Their acts were accompanied by special inward revelation and direction, unlike legislative revelation, which first prescribes and is then obeyed. Their prior worship of God confirms that this later revelation was inward support and strengthening; they were guided by the Holy Spirit and purity to do good, establish prayer, and give the alms required by their law. Al-Zamakhsharī’s attempt to treat these gerunds as passive objects of legislative revelation is rejected: a gerund used as an object is not equivalent to a conjugated verb, and its indication of realized acts cannot be the object of legislative revelation.

Lot received either judgment or wisdom, along with knowledge, and was saved from Sodom, whose people committed abominable acts and were evil transgressors. God’s mercy toward him may mean wilāyah or prophethood. Noah called upon his Lord before the prophets just discussed, and God answered him. His ahl are his close relatives excluding the wife and son who drowned, and the great calamity is profound sorrow. Finally, divine help against the deniers of God’s signs means deliverance from them; because they were an evil people, all were drowned.
verses.78: Al-Mizan recounts David and Solomon considering a case in which people’s sheep had pastured in a field by night, while God witnessed their judgment.
verses.79: Al-Mizan states that God made Solomon understand it, gave each one wisdom and knowledge, and subjected the mountains and birds to celebrate His praise with David.
verses.80: Al-Mizan says that God taught him to make coats of mail to protect people in war and calls them to gratitude.
verses.81: Al-Mizan states that God made the violently blowing wind subservient to Solomon, following his command toward the blessed land, while God knows all things.
verses.82: Al-Mizan says that some devils dived for him and performed other work, while God kept guard over them.
verses.83: Al-Mizan recounts Job’s cry to his Lord that harm had afflicted him, while God is the most Merciful of the merciful.

verses.88: Al-Mizan says that God answered, delivered him from grief, and thus delivers the believers.

verses.91:
Al-Mizan presents these prophets neither chronologically nor in reverse order: some are mentioned through particular divine blessings, while others are named alone.

Ḥarth denotes cultivation and can mean a vineyard, while nafsh is livestock spreading out to pasture at night without a herder. The case of David and Solomon concerned sheep that spoiled a field at night. Since David was Israel’s ruling king, the case was brought before him; Solomon’s participation was by his permission, perhaps to display his worthiness to succeed him. The progressive expression that they “were giving judgment” indicates consultation toward one decisive ruling, not two autonomous final judgments. Likewise, the plural pronoun in “their judgment” apparently refers to the prophets generally, all of whom receive ḥukm, rather than to the plaintiffs, to whom judgment cannot properly be ascribed. Their single judgment was apparently that the flock’s owner was liable for what it destroyed.

The commentary rejects both the claim that Solomon’s ruling abrogated David’s and the claim that each ruled by speculative ijtihād. Abrogation would require two distinct rulings, whereas the wording indicates one judgment; it would also make David’s ruling erroneous, despite God’s witness to it and His gift of wisdom and knowledge to each. Speculative ijtihād is still less plausible, because God made Solomon understand the true rule and confirms David’s knowledge as well. Their difference was therefore in applying and executing the same ruling, with Solomon’s application more exact and moderate. The reported Shiʿa and Sunni account is that David awarded the flock itself to the field owner, whereas Solomon awarded its milk, wool, and produce for that year. Perhaps both aimed at compensation equal to the destroyed crops: David used the livestock’s capital value, and Solomon more leniently used its annual yield, normally equivalent to that value. God’s witnessing means that He was present, seeing, hearing, and aiding them to follow the right path.

Imam al-Bāqir is reported to have said that David and Solomon were debating rather than issuing judgments. Abū Baṣīr reports from Imam al-Ṣādiq that nafsh occurs only at night: a field owner protects his field by day, but the livestock owner must restrain animals at night and is liable for their damage; David awarded the livestock, while Solomon awarded that year’s milk and wool. Another version from Imam al-Ṣādiq says David followed the ruling of previous prophets, then God revealed to Solomon that the field owner was entitled only to what came from the animals’ insides; this became a new practice, and each thus ruled by God’s ruling. In another report, Imam al-Ṣādiq calls the field a vineyard and says David’s ruling was intended to show the Israelites that Solomon would succeed him; they did not disagree, or the verse would have referred to two judgments. Majmaʿ al-bayān reports, from Imams al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq, that Solomon proposed giving the vines to the flock owner to restore them and the flock to the vineyard owner for its benefit until restoration, after which each property would return to its owner. The commentary adds that the vineyard description is also reported through Sunni chains from Ibn Masʿūd.

God subjected the mountains and birds with David to celebrate His praise. Taskhīr is not compulsion, coercion, or constraint: the subject acts in accordance with its own nature and choice, as fire burns when used or a hired person works. Thus the mountains’ and birds’ inherent praise was synchronized with David’s. God’s statement that He was the doer means that such gifts accord with His enduring custom and are not novel for Him.

God taught David to make labūs, understood here as armor or coats of mail, to protect people from the force of weapons in war; the closing question urges gratitude. Solomon’s violently blowing wind was made subservient to his command toward the blessed land, the Levant where he lived. Although the wind also served him gently, its violent state is mentioned because that subjection is more wondrous and more indicative of power. Some exegetes say the verse mentions travel to that land because he chiefly resided there, displaying God’s blessing; the commentary suggests it may instead mean that the wind moved toward the land in order to carry him from it wherever he wished, thus including both outward and return travel. Tafsīr al-Qummī identifies the blessed land as Jerusalem and the Levant, and says the wind blew from every direction.

The devils dived to obtain sea resources such as pearls and also undertook other works, including the construction of fortresses, images, great bowls, and immovable cooking-pots. God’s guarding them means retaining them in Solomon’s service and preventing escape, disobedience, and corruption of his affairs.

The harm denoted by ḍurr is harm especially afflicting one’s life, such as illness and emaciation, unlike ḍarr, which can mean any harm. Job lost his property and children and suffered prolonged severe bodily illness. After he called on God, God healed him and restored his property and children, together with their like. Giving him his family means restoring those children who had died; the event reminds worshipers that God tests His friends and then grants their reward without wasting that of the good-doers. Imam al-Ṣādiq is reported to have said that God brought back to life members of Job’s family who had died before and during his trial.

Ishmael, Idrīs, and Ezekiel are described as patient and good, admitted into divine mercy. Dhū al-Nūn is Jonah, who was swallowed by a great fish. He had called the people of Nineveh to God; after they disbelieved, he asked for punishment, but when they repented and believed before it descended, God removed it. Since Jonah had departed them, God tested him with the fish; he called upon God from its belly, was delivered, and was sent back to his people.

Jonah left in anger at his people’s unbelief. “We would not straiten him” can mean that he did not think God would tighten his provision, as qadara may mean to restrict. It may also be analogical: his departure resembled a slave’s angry flight from a master whom he thinks cannot control him. It cannot mean that Jonah truly believed God lacked power over him or that he was angry with God, for that is indubitably remote from prophets, who are protected by divine infallibility. The darknesses may be those of the sea, the fish’s belly, and the night. His declaration that none is god but God dissociated him from the appearance that he could turn to refuge apart from his Lord; glorifying God dissociated him from the appearance of criticizing God’s action, being angered by it, or escaping His power. His confession of wrongdoing acknowledges an action resembling wrongdoing, not actual sin or intended disobedience. It was divine discipline, clearing his will of even the semblance of wrongdoing so that he might tread the path of nearness.

Though Jonah did not expressly ask for deliverance, his declaration of God’s unity and purity and his confession expressed his condition before his Lord and implicitly sought relief. Deliverance from grief is therefore also a promise for believers tested by grief who call upon God similarly. Imam al-Bāqir is reported to explain that Jonah thought he would not be punished for what he was doing. Imam al-Riḍā reports that ẓanna here means certainty: Jonah was certain that God would not straiten his provision, for if he had believed God lacked power over him he would have been an unbeliever. Imam al-Ṣādiq reportedly identifies Jonah’s supplication as the Qur’anic remedy for sorrow and worry, supported by God’s promise to deliver believers; the same meaning is also reported from him in al-Khiṣāl through an incomplete chain. Saʿd reports that the Messenger of God said Jonah’s supplication is a divine name by which God answers and grants petitions: it was Jonah’s in particular but also belongs to believers who invoke God by it, as shown by “and thus do We deliver the believers.”

Zechariah’s plea not to be left alone asks for a child and inheritor. Calling God the best of inheritors is both praise and a declaration that, although Zechariah sought an heir, God inherits all things and has no partner or equal in inheritance. God gave him John and made his wife fit for him, apparently by making her young and fertile after barrenness. The pronoun concerning those who hastened in good deeds refers to Zechariah’s household, and explains their blessing: they competed in good works, prayed hoping for divine mercy or reward and fearing wrath or punishment, and their hearts were humble before divine grandeur. The phrase may alternatively describe them as those who hoped and feared. Tafsīr al-Qummī reports that Zechariah’s wife began menstruating after not doing so, and glosses raghaban wa rahaban as those who hope and fear. Imam Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar is reported to define raghbah in supplication as raising the palms heavenward toward the face, and rahbah as raising the palms downward and lifting the hands toward the face; a similar report from Imam al-Ṣādiq says raghbah directs the palms heavenward and rahbah the backs of the hands heavenward.

“She who guarded her chastity” is Mary daughter of ʿImrān. The description praises her chastity and immaculateness and refutes the Jews’ accusation against her. Breathing the spirit into her indirectly signifies that Jesus was not born through the ordinary process of conception followed by the breathing of spirit into a zygote. With no conception, there was only the breathing of the spirit—the divine word—into her, like Adam’s creation by the command “Be”; both creations were without fertilized sperm. Tafsīr al-Qummī reports that no being saw Mary and identifies the spirit as created, belonging to God’s command. Mary and her son are one sign for all nations: the singular “sign” joins them in the extraordinary birth of Jesus, which depends upon both. Mary is named first because she preceded Jesus in time. Although she was not a prophet, her mention among the prophets in God’s Book is itself ample honor.

verses.112:
Al-Mizan reads these verses as returning to the chapter’s governing call: humanity has one Creator and Lord, and therefore one religion, monotheism, to which all prophets summon. Responding to prophethood prepares people for the Day of Reckoning. Though people have fractured this unified religion into rival creeds, made other gods, and pursued divergent ends, the righteous will receive abiding comfort and honour, whereas the wicked face punishment, destruction, and the loss of their efforts. In this world as well, God promises the righteous the good end and inheritance of the earth.

For (21:92), ummah means the whole human species, a group joined by one purpose and destination, and the address is universal to accountable human beings. Since humanity is one special reality, governed by one interconnected creative order and directed toward one happy human life, it can have only one real regulator and Lord. Lordship is not an honorary office that people may distribute among whichever gods they choose; it is the existential governance of human affairs. Thus the one human species must worship its true Owner and Director, God alone. Al-Mizan rejects the view that ummah here metaphorically means the religion of islām shared by all prophets: there is no reason to leave the literal meaning, and that reading neither fits the relevant usage of ummah nor explains why the verse says rabb rather than ilāh.

For (21:93), whether taqaṭṭuʿ is understood as cutting up, becoming divided in their affair, or making their affair divided, the expression depicts people breaking the single religion of monotheism conveyed through prophethood into fragments, each taking part and abandoning the rest. This rebukes the idolaters, Jews, Christians, Zoroastrians, Sabeans, and their sects for abandoning the command to worship God alone. Their division is not without consequence: all return to God to be requited according to their differing ways. The final clause answers the implicit question of where this religious disagreement ends.

Verse (21:94) concerns their Hereafter. Good deeds are accepted only with belief; in this context, belief in God necessarily includes belief in all His messengers without distinction. God will not cover over or fail to appreciate the believer’s exertion, but will record it in the scrolls of deeds without forgetting it. The verse therefore indicates both the futility of good deeds with disbelief and the salvation of a believer who performs some good deeds.

The primary contextual sense of (21:95) is that people of a town destroyed by God cannot return to worldly life to make up the works they missed. They represent the opposite of believers whose works are accepted: having lacked belief and good deeds, they have no recorded or appreciated effort and no second worldly life in which to recover their loss. The verse speaks of a town because individual corruption may spread into social rebellion until a community deserves destruction. A remote possibility is that destruction means the sinful loss of capacity for guidance and felicity, so that a town is barred from repentance and uprightness. On either reading, it cannot return to compensate for what it missed. The wording that they are banned “that they shall not return” is a rational metaphor: it names the immediate result of the prohibition, making their non-return appear already established. Al-Mizan considers the readings that treat the negative particle as superfluous, make ḥarām mean obligatory, supply a different object for the ban, or take the phrase as denying resurrection, weak.

Verse (21:96) marks the endpoint of this course of reward and destruction: Gog and Magog will be let loose when the barrier holding them back is opened, and they will rush swiftly down from every elevated place. This is among the conditions of the Hour and signs of the Resurrection. Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation, attributed to Mujāhid, that the pronoun refers to people emerging from graves. It conflicts with the surrounding references to Gog and Magog and the approaching true promise; grammatically the clause describes Gog and Magog’s condition; and emergence from every height does not suit graves, even if a variant reading changes “elevated place” to “grave.”

In (21:97), the true promise is the Hour. The unbelievers’ fixed, unblinking gaze expresses their undistracted alarm at a sudden evil event. On seeing the Hour, they first cry that they had been heedless, as though their heedlessness had been imposed on them; then they acknowledge that they themselves were unjust, having immersed themselves in worldly concerns that caused forgetfulness of the Hereafter.

For (21:98), ḥaṣab means fuel or what is cast into a fire. The use of mā, “what you worship,” confines the condemned objects of worship to idols and images, excluding such beings as prophets, saints, and angels; the later exception for those granted the good promise confirms this. The address apparently occurs on the Day of Resurrection, when unbelievers and their gods are sentenced to Hell, rather than being a worldly argument against idolatry. The lām in lahā may emphasize the direct verb or mean “to,” and the address includes both worshippers and their gods. Verse (21:99) exposes the false gods’ reality: if they were gods, they would not enter Hell, yet both they and their worshippers remain there forever. In (21:100), zafīr is the harsh sound of inhaling, likened to a donkey’s braying. The unbelievers’ inability to hear is punishment for refusing the word of truth in the world, just as lost sight punishes refusal to reflect on divine signs. The change away from directly addressing them displays their miserable state to others, and the pronouns here concern the unbelievers alone.

The good already decreed for those in (21:101) is the best promise: deliverance and Paradise. Those granted it will be removed far from Hell. They will not hear even its faintest perceptible sound, will abide in what they desire, and the greatest terror will not grieve them. The angels will meet them with glad tidings: this is their promised day.

For (21:104), al-sijill is most simply the scroll or sheet upon which writing appears. As writings vanish from view when their scroll is rolled up, heaven will be rolled up by divine power so that neither it nor its trace is visible. It does not thereby vanish from the unseen, just as hidden writing remains on its scroll. This can signify the heavens’ return to the treasuries of the unseen from which things were sent down in measure. On that basis, “as We originated the first creation, We shall return it” may mean return to the state before creation, when things were nothing worthy of mention. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās likewise says that everything will perish as it was at the beginning. Al-Mizan finds this plausible for the rolling up of heaven, but holds that the immediate context more apparently means resurrection: God will bring creation back to life as easily as He originated it. This is a binding divine promise that He will surely fulfill.

In (21:105), Zabūr apparently denotes David’s scripture, and “the reminder” the Torah; proposed identifications of either term with the Qur’an, every revealed scripture, scripture after Moses, or the Guarded Tablet lack evidence. Inheriting the earth is receiving control of its benefits without transaction. It applies without restriction to worldly and otherworldly inheritance. Worldly inheritance means a righteous human society enjoying the earth after it is cleansed of polytheism and disobedience, serving God without partners. Otherworldly inheritance consists in the enduring nearness, bliss, and comfort that the righteous acquire through their worldly life. Al-Mizan therefore rejects confining the verse solely to the Hereafter or solely to the world. Those who confine it to the world connect it with Islam’s eventual prevalence or the Mahdi’s appearance, supported, they say, by mutawātir reports transmitted by both Shias and Sunnis. The verse is more naturally linked to (21:94) and following, however: after distinguishing believers and unbelievers in their Hereafter, it also distinguishes their worldly outcome—the righteous inherit the earth, unlike the others.

Verse (21:106) says that the chapter’s teaching is sufficient for, and brings to their aim, people who serve God: it establishes the one Lord, service through prophethood in preparation for reckoning, and the respective recompense of believers and unbelievers. In (21:107), the plural, definite al-ʿālamīn establishes the universality of the Prophet’s mission. He is mercy to all human communities because his religion, if adopted, brings worldly and otherworldly happiness, and because the truthful call produces beneficial effects in human society.

For (21:108), the double exclusivity means that the revealed religion is nothing but monotheism. Both belief and religious rulings either follow from it or return to it. If people turn away, verses (21:109-110) command the Prophet to tell them that he has equally informed and warned them of their danger, not specifically warned them of war, a reading unsuitable to a Meccan chapter. He must also deny knowing whether the threatened punishment is near or far. God alone knows their outward mockery and criticism of Islam as well as their concealed plots against it; therefore only He knows the measure of their crime and the time its punishment warrants.

Verse (21:111) continues this commanded speech. “This” perhaps refers indirectly to the warning: it may be a trial exposing their true attitude toward the call, while their temporary enjoyment is respite (imhāl) and/or gradual leading into temptation and perdition (istidrāj). The Prophet then asks in (21:112) that his Lord judge with truth after their persistent rejection. “With truth” does not restrict God’s judgment, since it is always true; it asks God to manifest His true judgment for the followers of truth against its opponents. He again addresses the polytheists by calling God “our Lord”: God is Lord of both sides and settles disputes among His servants. As the Beneficent, He does not refuse one who petitions Him; His judgment cannot be deferred, and He establishes truth and removes falsehood. The prayer thus seeks His merciful aid against their false ascriptions, including praising their own religion with virtues it lacks and imputing to the religion of truth vices from which it is free. The shifts from second to third person, from “my Lord” to “our Lord,” and the descriptions “the Beneficent” and “Whose help is sought” accord with this movement of the address.
